examples.title: A client connects and says nothing
examples.request: TCP connect to the port named by `-accept`; the client sends no bytes
examples.response: Nothing on the wire. The socket stays open and the server waits for a ClientHello.
examples.note: TLS is strictly client-speaks-first: the ClientHello is the first byte either side sends. A server that writes a greeting on accept, or that closes an idle socket immediately, fails this stage.

examples.title: A client connects and disconnects without a ClientHello
examples.request: TCP connect, then an immediate FIN
examples.response: The server closes that socket and goes back to accepting. Nothing is logged as fatal and the process keeps running.
examples.note: Port scanners and health checks do this all day. `read()` returning 0 before a ClientHello is the end of a connection, not an error to abort on.

stages.name: Record size limits
hints: TLSPlaintext.length may not exceed 2^14 (16384); a longer one is a record_overflow alert, not a bigger buffer
Check the length field before allocating: a two-byte length can ask for 65535 bytes that will never arrive
TLSCiphertext may be 2^14 + 256, which leaves room for the content type, the padding and the AEAD tag
A record that promises more bytes than the client ever sends must time out or close, never spin or wedge the accept loop

examples.note: The removal is deliberate: renegotiation carried a decade of attacks, from RFC 5746's prefix injection to the triple handshake. There is no compatible way back and none is wanted.

stages.name: Fifty connections at once
hints: Every connection needs its own state: keys, sequence numbers, transcript and read buffer. Anything shared between them is a bug waiting for load
A server may serve connections one at a time or in parallel; both are conformant, and both must finish all fifty
Never let one slow or stuck client stop the accept loop — a listen backlog is not a queue you can ignore
Close each connection's socket when it ends rather than when the process does, or a long-lived server runs out of file descriptors

tests.name: fifty connections opened at once all complete
each connection gets its own answer, never another's
fifty sequential connections all complete
connections that are opened and abandoned do not block the others
two hundred connect-and-close cycles leak nothing
the server still serves a clean handshake afterwards

examples.title: What each of the fifty connections does
examples.request: A full handshake, then `conn00\n` as application data, then close_notify
examples.response: `00nnoc\n`, and a close_notify back.
examples.note: Fifty of these at once. Nothing about any one of them is unusual — the test is whether the fiftieth is as correct as the first.

request_fields.value: 24 bytes: the AEAD ciphertext plus its 16-byte tag. The real content type is inside it, after the content and before the padding.

response_fields.value: 24 bytes: the AEAD ciphertext plus its 16-byte tag. The real content type is inside it, after the content and before the padding.

examples.title: Serial and parallel are both fine
examples.request: Fifty sockets opened before any of them has finished its handshake
examples.response: A threaded server serves them at once; a single-threaded one serves them from the listen backlog in turn. Both finish all fifty.
examples.note: The reference is single-threaded, so this suite never requires two handshakes to be in flight at the same moment — only that opening fifty sockets does not lose any of them.

stages.name: Fuzz: four hundred mutated hellos
hints: Validate every length against the bytes you actually have before you index — that one rule survives most of this stage
A malformed input is at worst a closed connection: never a panic, never an unbounded allocation, never a loop that does not end
The accept loop has to outlive every bad connection; test that by sending a clean handshake afterwards, which is what this stage does
Everything here comes from --seed, so a failure is reproducible: the report names the round and the mutation that broke it

tests.name: four hundred mutated ClientHellos leave the server standing
every mutation kind is survivable on its own
a hundred records of pure noise are survivable
mutations after a completed handshake are survivable
the same seed produces the same corpus
a clean handshake still works after all of it

examples.title: One of the four hundred: a hello cut to a third
examples.request: The first third of a perfectly good ClientHello record. The header promises far more than follows.
examples.response: Nothing, or an alert, and then a close. The next connection is accepted as though nothing had happened.
examples.note: The other seven mutations are a flipped bit, a length replaced with 0xffff, a length replaced with zero, a run of noise, a duplicated slice, an undefined content type and an undefined handshake type.

examples.title: What a fuzz failure looks like
examples.request: `tlstest --server my_server --stage 40 --seed 0x1234`
examples.response: The report names the round and the mutation: 'round 137 (a length field replaced with 0xffff)'. The same seed replays the same corpus exactly.
examples.note: Reproducibility is the whole value. Re-run with `--seed` and the same bytes come back, so the crash can be debugged rather than described.

stages.name: HelloRetryRequest
hints: A HelloRetryRequest *is* a ServerHello: same message type, same fields, and a random fixed at SHA-256("HelloRetryRequest")
Its key_share carries only a selected_group and no share; the client answers with a second ClientHello carrying a share for that group
Before the retry goes into the transcript, ClientHello1 is replaced by the synthetic `message_hash` message of RFC 8446 section 4.4.1 — this is the one rule nobody guesses
A cookie, if one is sent, must be echoed back verbatim in the second hello and nowhere else

tests.name: a hello with no key share earns a HelloRetryRequest
the retry's random is SHA-256 of "HelloRetryRequest"
the retry names a group the client offered
the retry carries supported_versions and a key_share of two bytes
the handshake completes after the retry
the transcript uses the synthetic message_hash message
a cookie, if one is sent, is echoed in the second hello
data flows on a connection that began with a retry

examples.title: The retry request itself
examples.request: A ClientHello naming x25519 and secp256r1 in supported_groups, with an empty key_share list
examples.response: A ServerHello whose random is CF 21 AD 74 … 33 9C and whose key_share holds two bytes: the group it wants.
examples.note: Look at the random in the hex: it is not random at all. Any ServerHello carrying SHA-256("HelloRetryRequest") is a retry, and the client must not treat it as a completed key exchange.

examples.title: The transcript after a retry
examples.request:
Transcript-Hash(ClientHello1, HelloRetryRequest, ClientHello2, ...) =
Hash( message_hash || 00 00 Hash.length || Hash(ClientHello1)
      || HelloRetryRequest || ClientHello2 || ... )
examples.response: `message_hash` is handshake type 254, and the three length bytes are the hash length — 00 00 20 for SHA-256, 00 00 30 for SHA-384.
examples.note: The replacement lets a stateless server reconstruct the transcript from the cookie alone: it never has to remember ClientHello1, only its hash. Skip it and every retried handshake dies at the server's Finished.

stages.name: KeyUpdate
hints: The body is one byte: update_not_requested(0) or update_requested(1)
The new secret is HKDF-Expand-Label(old secret, "traffic upd", "", Hash.length); key and iv are expanded from it exactly as before
Only the sender's own direction changes, and the sequence number goes back to zero; the KeyUpdate itself is the last record under the old keys
update_requested(1) obliges the peer to send its own KeyUpdate back — and that answer must say update_not_requested, or two peers would ping-pong for ever

tests.name: data keeps flowing after update_not_requested
update_requested earns a KeyUpdate back
the write keys really change
the sequence number resets on the updated direction
several updates in a row all work
a KeyUpdate with an undefined request_update is refused
a KeyUpdate with a body of the wrong length is refused

examples.title: A line before the keys rotate
examples.request: `rotate\n` under application_traffic_secret_0
examples.response: `etator\n` back. A `18 00 00 01 00` KeyUpdate follows, and then the same exchange works under secret_1.
examples.note: The KeyUpdate message is five bytes: type 24, a uint24 length of 1, and the request_update byte. Everything else about it is derivation.

response_fields.value: 24 bytes: the AEAD ciphertext plus its 16-byte tag. The real content type is inside it, after the content and before the padding.

examples.title: What a KeyUpdate changes, and what it does not
examples.request:
secret_(N+1) = HKDF-Expand-Label(secret_N, "traffic upd", "", Hash.length)
key, iv      = HKDF-Expand-Label(secret_(N+1), "key"/"iv", "", ...)
sequence number -> 0
examples.response: Only the sender's direction moves. The transcript is untouched, the master secret is untouched, and no new key exchange happens.
examples.note: update_requested(1) asks the peer to rotate too, and its answer must say update_not_requested(0). Two peers that both say 1 would never stop.

stages.name: NewSessionTicket and resumption
hints: A ticket's PSK is HKDF-Expand-Label(resumption_master_secret, "resumption", ticket_nonce, Hash.length) — the nonce is what makes two tickets from one connection different
pre_shared_key must be the *last* extension of the ClientHello, because the binder is computed over everything before it
binder = HMAC(finished_key(binder_key), Transcript-Hash(truncated ClientHello)), where the truncation stops just before the binder list's own length
A resumed handshake sends no Certificate and no CertificateVerify: the PSK is the authentication

tests.name: the server sends a NewSessionTicket
the ticket's fields are well-formed
two tickets from one connection have different nonces
a ticket resumes the session
a resumed handshake sends no Certificate
data flows on a resumed connection
a wrong binder does not resume
an unknown ticket falls back to a full handshake

examples.title: A NewSessionTicket
examples.request: The client's Finished, which is what the resumption secret is taken over
examples.response: `04`, a uint24 length, ticket_lifetime, ticket_age_add, a ticket_nonce, the opaque ticket itself, and an extensions block.
examples.note: The ticket is opaque to the client: it is whatever the server needs to recover the PSK, usually its own state sealed under a key only it holds.

response_fields.value: 0xbaf7cf14 — added to the client's ticket age so it cannot be correlated
dea6970a6d0a8343… (208 bytes) — opaque to the client; it becomes the PSK identity
0 — an `early_data` extension here would carry max_early_data_size

examples.title: The binder, step by step
examples.request:
binder_key   = Derive-Secret(Early Secret, "res binder", "")
finished_key = HKDF-Expand-Label(binder_key, "finished", "", Hash.length)
binder       = HMAC(finished_key, Transcript-Hash(Truncate(ClientHello)))
examples.response: Truncate() stops just before the binder list's two-byte length — everything from `01` to the end of the identities is hashed, and nothing after.
examples.note: The Early Secret here is HKDF-Extract(0, PSK), not the zero-PSK one: the binder proves the client knows the PSK before the server has spent anything on it.

stages.name: Early data, offered and refused
hints: Early data is only on offer when the *ticket* said so: a NewSessionTicket with no early_data extension means 0-RTT is not available on it
A client may send early_data in its hello anyway; a server that does not want it simply leaves early_data out of EncryptedExtensions
When early data is refused there is no EndOfEarlyData message — that only exists on a connection where the server accepted it
Refusing is always safe and often right: 0-RTT data is replayable, and RFC 8446 appendix E.5 spends several pages on why

tests.name: a ticket without early_data does not permit 0-RTT
offering early_data anyway still completes the handshake
the server does not accept early data it never advertised
EncryptedExtensions carries no early_data extension
no EndOfEarlyData is expected on a refused connection
data flows normally after early data was refused
offering early_data without a PSK is ignored

examples.title: A hello offering early_data, and the refusal
examples.request: An ordinary ClientHello with an extra extension: type 42, length 0. The extension is a flag and carries no body.
examples.response: EncryptedExtensions with no early_data extension in it. That absence is the whole refusal — there is no alert and nothing to retry.
examples.note: Offering costs the client nothing. A server that does not want 0-RTT says so by saying nothing, and the connection carries on as a normal 1-RTT handshake.

request_fields.value: 0x0303 (TLS 1.3 pins this at 0x0303; the real version is in supported_versions)
a10957883bae1ce0b73943bcf12d5b4ef35620e53413bf357fc5ba1d17344bbb (the server must echo this back byte for byte)
2e7db5c9e0184ce1… (32 bytes) — the client's ephemeral public key
empty — this extension is a flag

examples.title: Why refusing is the sane default
examples.request: 0-RTT data is sent before the server has said anything, so it cannot be bound to a fresh exchange.
examples.response: An attacker who captures it can replay it, and the server cannot tell the copy from the original without state it may not have.
examples.note: RFC 8446 appendix E.5 is explicit: applications must not use 0-RTT for anything non-idempotent. Advertising it is opt-in per ticket, and refusing an offer is always allowed.

stages.name: Real-client interop
hints: The suite's own client is one implementation; a second, independent one is the only way to find the places where both of yours agree and the RFC does not
`openssl s_client -tls1_3 -connect host:port` is the shortest full TLS 1.3 client there is, and it prints the negotiated parameters
Its `-ciphersuites` and `-groups` flags pin the negotiation, so each of the three suites and both groups can be exercised from the outside
`-sess_out` then `-sess_in` proves resumption end to end: the second run prints `Reused` when the ticket was accepted

tests.name: openssl s_client completes a handshake
openssl s_client gets its line reversed
openssl s_client reports TLSv1.3
openssl s_client negotiates each of the three suites
openssl s_client negotiates over secp256r1 as well as x25519
openssl s_client verifies the certificate against its own CA file
openssl s_client resumes with a ticket
curl over this contract is not a meaningful test
the suite's own client still works after all of that

examples.title: The shortest independent client there is
examples.request: printf 'interop\n' | openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:PORT -tls1_3 -quiet
examples.response: `ponretni` on stdout. With `-quiet` dropped, s_client also prints the negotiated protocol, cipher suite, temp key and certificate chain.
examples.note: This is the test that catches the bugs two implementations by the same author agree on. Run it early and often — it costs one command line.

examples.title: Pinning the negotiation from the outside
examples.request:
-ciphersuites TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256   pins the suite
-groups secp256r1                            pins the group
-sess_out f / -sess_in f                     saves and resumes a session
-CAfile cert.pem -verify_return_error        makes verification fatal
examples.response: Each flag exercises one negotiation path end to end, with an implementation that has no idea what your server does internally.
examples.note: `curl --tlsv1.3` is deliberately not used here: this track's contract is a line-reversing echo, not HTTP, so curl would have nothing meaningful to say.

stages.name: CertificateRequest
hints: CertificateRequest is handshake type 13 and belongs in the encrypted flight, after EncryptedExtensions and before the server's own Certificate

Its body is certificate_request_context (opaque<0..255>, empty during a handshake) followed by an extensions block — there is no certificate_types or supported_signature_algorithms list any more, those were TLS 1.2
signature_algorithms is mandatory in it: without it the client has no way to know what it may sign with, so an empty extensions block is an illegal message
Sending it at all is a choice; a server that never wants client certificates simply omits the message and nothing else about the handshake changes

tests.name: the server sends one when it is asking
it arrives inside the encrypted flight
it comes before the server's own Certificate
the context is empty during a handshake
it carries signature_algorithms
the schemes it offers are ones a TLS 1.3 client can use
requiring a certificate looks the same on the wire as requesting one
a server that was not asked for client auth sends none

examples.title: A CertificateRequest, field by field
examples.request: An ordinary ClientHello, against a server that wants a client certificate
examples.response: `0d`, a uint24 length, `00` for the empty certificate_request_context, then a uint16-counted extensions block holding signature_algorithms(13).
examples.note: Two bytes of context and a list of schemes is the whole message: TLS 1.2's certificate_types and its own copy of the CA list are gone. Note where it sits — after EncryptedExtensions, before the server's Certificate, and encrypted, so nobody watching the connection can tell that client authentication is in play.

stages.name: The client's Certificate and CertificateVerify
hints: Both messages go out under the *client* handshake traffic keys, after the server's Finished and before the client's own
The client's Certificate echoes the certificate_request_context byte for byte — empty during a handshake, but echoing is the rule

CertificateVerify signs 64 spaces, then "TLS 1.3, client CertificateVerify", then a zero byte, then the transcript hash up to and including the client's Certificate — a different context string from the server's, on purpose
The client's Certificate and CertificateVerify are in the transcript, so the Finished that follows covers them and its verify_data differs from an unauthenticated handshake's

and the data path still works afterwards
the client's Certificate echoes the request context
the CertificateVerify uses a scheme the server offered
the client's messages are in the transcript before its Finished

a certificate the server's CA never signed is refused

examples.note: The same message shape the server sent, in the other direction. The context byte is copied from the request rather than assumed empty.

a DER X.509 certificate — entry 0 is the end-entity certificate, and each later entry certifies the one before it
0 — every entry carries its own extensions block, new in TLS 1.3

examples.title: The client's CertificateVerify
examples.request: The certificate whose key is about to be proven

examples.note: The signature is over 64 spaces, then "TLS 1.3, client CertificateVerify", then a zero byte, then the transcript hash taken *after* the Certificate above. Getting the context string or the hash boundary wrong produces a signature that is perfectly valid over the wrong thing, which is why the server's rejection is decrypt_error rather than a decode error.

stages.name: Declining, and requesting against requiring
hints: Declining is an empty Certificate, not silence: the client still sends the message, with a zero-length certificate_list, and no CertificateVerify after it
A server that only *requests* must carry on with an unauthenticated connection — the handshake completes and application data flows
A server that *requires* must fail the handshake, and certificate_required(116) is the alert that says why; handshake_failure loses that information
An empty Certificate is followed by Finished and nothing else — a CertificateVerify with no certificate to verify is an illegal message

and says certificate_required rather than something vaguer
